explanations.explanation: Verse 1 says it plainly: the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites. Achan, the man from Judah, is the one who took the devoted things. Yet the verse opens by saying the Israelites acted unfaithfully regarding them. I think that's the line that makes you stop and read it twice.

I see why you landed there, because Achan is the one named as taking the things. But the verse says the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites. It also begins by saying the Israelites acted unfaithfully. So the text points wider than one man.
Jericho's wall has already fallen by this point (Joshua 6:20). This verse turns the other way. It says the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites, not against Jericho's people.
Close, but it's the opposite. The spies tell Joshua there is no need to send all the people. They say two or three thousand men are enough. The spies bring back a smaller plan, not a bigger one.

That's right. The spies say there's no need to send all the people, and that two or three thousand men are enough. They say the people of Ai are so few that Joshua need not wear out everyone. That's the exact confidence I have right before I say I'll only glance away from the oven for a second.

explanations.answer: They flee before the men of Ai
explanations.explanation: Verse 4 says about three thousand men went up, but they fled before the men of Ai. After Jericho, nobody on that road expected running. The spies called Ai few, and the men of Ai still sent them off the field.

explanations.answer: They capture Ai in one day
explanations.explanation: That's what the spies' plan sounded like, and Jericho's wall had just fallen (Joshua 6:20), so I get the feeling. But the text says the men went up and fled before the men of Ai. No capturing happens here.
It goes the other way. The men of Ai are the ones sending Israel running, and they strike down about thirty-six of them. Nobody in this scene is surrendering.
The text says the hearts of the people melted and became like water. That's a picture of courage running right out of them. About thirty-six men were lost, and the whole people felt it.
It's actually true. Verse 5 says the hearts of the people melted and became like water. The loss at Ai hit the whole people, not just the men who fled.

explanations.answer: Stayed on the other side of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Joshua says, “If only we had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan!” (Joshua 7:7). That's a man at his lowest saying out loud what he's feeling. I think his heart is just about on the floor.

explanations.answer: Stayed back in the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Joshua never mentions Egypt here. He says he wishes they had been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan. The river he's talking about is the one they had just crossed.

explanations.answer: Waited longer in the camp at Jericho
explanations.explanation: Joshua doesn't say anything about waiting at Jericho. His wish is about the other side of the Jordan. He's looking back past the whole crossing.

explanations.answer: Surround Israel and wipe out its name
explanations.explanation: Joshua says the Canaanites and all who live in the land will hear about this. Then, in his words, “they will surround us and wipe out our name from the earth.” He's looking ahead and he doesn't like what he sees. A lost battle feels like the start of something bigger.
Joshua is afraid in the other direction. He says the Canaanites will surround Israel and wipe out its name. The people of the land are the ones he's worried about.
Joshua doesn't picture peace talks. He says they will surround Israel and wipe out its name from the earth. That's a much darker guess about what Ai's news will do.
He ends with a question to God: “Then what will You do for Your great name?” He brings the whole mess straight to the LORD. He doesn't hide it or dress it up.
It's actually true. Joshua closes his prayer by asking, “Then what will You do for Your great name?” His last words go to the LORD, not to the people.

explanations.answer: They have been set apart for destruction
explanations.explanation: The LORD says the Israelites will turn their backs and run because they themselves have been set apart for destruction. That's the reason He gives for why they can't stand against their enemies. Notice He points at what's among them, not at Ai.

explanations.answer: They have forgotten how to fight
explanations.explanation: The LORD never says anything about forgetting how to fight. He says they cannot stand against their enemies because they themselves have been set apart for destruction. The problem He names is among them.

explanations.answer: Their enemies have grown too strong
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say the enemy got stronger. He says the Israelites cannot stand because they themselves have been set apart for destruction. The cause He points to is inside the camp.
The LORD says, “I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction.” That's about as clear as it gets. Everything depends on removing it.
It's actually true. The LORD says, “I will no longer be with you unless you remove from among you whatever is devoted to destruction.” He puts it right on the table.

explanations.answer: The LORD selects tribe by tribe down to one man
explanations.explanation: The LORD says the tribe He selects comes forward clan by clan, then family by family, then man by man. The circle keeps shrinking until it lands on one man. Nobody has to guess who it is.

explanations.answer: Joshua has every tent in the camp searched
explanations.explanation: No tent search is the plan here. The LORD lays out tribe, clan, family and man. The messengers only run to a tent later, after Achan names where the things are hidden (Joshua 7:21-22).

explanations.answer: Joshua has every man come and confess
explanations.explanation: Joshua doesn't line up every man to confess. The LORD says the selecting goes tribe by tribe down to one man. Joshua urges a confession only after Achan has been selected (Joshua 7:18-19).

explanations.answer: He transgressed the covenant of the LORD
explanations.explanation: The LORD says it's because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD and committed an outrage in Israel. That's the reason given, and it's about the covenant. The text is heavy here, and the reason it gives is plain.

explanations.answer: He ran away from the battle at Ai
explanations.explanation: Fleeing at Ai is what the three thousand men did, but it's not the reason the LORD gives here. He says it's because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD. The charge is about what he took, not about running.

explanations.answer: He refused to march around Jericho
explanations.explanation: Marching around Jericho isn't part of what the LORD says here. The reason in verse 15 is that he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD and committed an outrage in Israel. It's all about the devoted things.
Joshua says, “give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him.” Then he adds that Achan should not hide it from him. Hiding is over, and telling the truth is on the table.
Joshua isn't asking for an offering. He asks Achan to give glory to the LORD and make a confession to Him. He wants Achan to tell what he did.
A promise would be about the future, but Joshua asks for something else. He says to give glory to the LORD and make a confession to Him. He wants to hear what Achan has done.

explanations.answer: A cloak and silver and a gold bar
explanations.explanation: Achan says he saw a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels. He lists exactly what he took, down to the weights. When it all comes out, he's very specific.

explanations.answer: A crown and a sword and a shield
explanations.explanation: Achan doesn't mention a crown, a sword or a shield. He names a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels.

explanations.answer: Bronze pots and a few iron tools
explanations.explanation: No pots or tools in his list. Achan says he took a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels.
Achan says, “I coveted them and took them.” He sees something beautiful and wants it, and then his hands follow. He names it himself, and I think that took a lot of nerve.
Achan never says he needed anything. He says, “I coveted them and took them.” He names his own wanting.
Fear isn't the word he uses. Achan says he saw the things, coveted them and took them. He owns up to wanting them.

Not quite. Achan says the things are hidden in the ground inside his tent, with the silver underneath. They were in the middle of the camp, not outside it. The messengers find them just where he says.
That's right. Achan says they are hidden in the ground inside his tent, with the silver underneath. Nothing was buried outside the camp. The messengers run to the tent and find it all.

explanations.answer: Spread them out before the LORD
explanations.explanation: They took the things from inside the tent, brought them to Joshua and all the Israelites, and spread them out before the LORD. Everything that had been hidden is now out in the open. Nothing is left underneath anything.

explanations.answer: Put them in the LORD's treasury
explanations.explanation: No treasury here. The text says they spread the things out before the LORD. The hidden things are laid out in plain sight.

explanations.answer: Bury them back in the ground
explanations.explanation: Burying was how Achan hid them, in the ground inside his tent. This time they take the things out of the tent and spread them out before the LORD. Hiding is over.

The text says the opposite. After this, the LORD turned from His burning anger. This part of the story is hard to read, and I think it's okay to feel that. Verse 26 closes the matter by saying the LORD turned.
That's right. Verse 26 says the LORD turned from His burning anger. The place is called the Valley of Achor to this day. This one is heavy, and the text still tells us where the anger ends.
